title: Ireland Beat India for the First Time in Thirty Years of Trying. The World Champions Lost by 34 Runs.
excerpt: Belfast's Civil Service Cricket Club hosted one of the biggest upsets in T20I history as Ireland dismantled India's post-World Cup line-up. The second T20I is today.
body:
For thirty years and sixteen matches across every format of the game, Ireland had never beaten India. On Friday evening in Belfast, playing at a tiny ground with a capacity smaller than most school stadiums in Mumbai, they did it — by 34 runs — and the world champions did not look close.

India's T20I winning streak of twelve consecutive series or tournament victories is over. So is the illusion that the post-World Cup transition — new captain Shreyas Iyer, new vice-captain Tilak Varma, the controversial axing of Suryakumar Yadav — would be seamless.

## How Ireland Won

On a slow Belfast pitch where 128 is the average first-innings total, Ireland posted 182 for 9 — forty runs above the ground's historical norm. They did it by absorbing early damage and then accelerating through the middle overs.

India's seamers did the early work, reducing the hosts to 30 for 3 with Tim Tector, Ross Adair, and Harry Tector all falling cheaply. But captain Lorcan Tucker, who would finish with a composed fifty, and Gareth Delany, who smashed 49 off 32 balls with three fours and three sixes, stitched together a 64-run partnership for the fifth wicket that shifted the match.

The acceleration was clinical. Delany played the role of controlled destroyer, timing his assault on the short straight boundaries with precision. Tucker anchored, rotated, and then cut loose at the death. Ireland's tail squeezed 40 runs from the final four overs to post a total that looked steep on a surface offering lateral movement and uneven bounce.

## India's Collapse

The reply began at a blistering pace. Abhishek Sharma, the left-handed opener, smashed seven fours and two sixes to reach 50 off just 19 balls — one of the fastest half-centuries in India's T20I history. At 70 for 1 in the eighth over, India looked comfortable.

Then Sharma fell to Liam McCarthy, and the middle order came apart. Matt Hollard, a medium-pacer who would not trouble most IPL line-ups, took three wickets in his four overs — Ishan Kishan, captain Shreyas Iyer, and all-rounder Washington Sundar — as India's pursuit lost structure and then collapsed entirely.

The last eight wickets fell for 78 runs. India were bowled out for 148 in 18.5 overs.

## Tactical Questions for India

Head coach Gautam Gambhir — who has already overseen India's first Test series whitewash at home in twelve years — now faces pointed questions about squad selection and bowling deployment.

The decision to introduce Washington Sundar for the first time as late as the 16th over, against two set right-hand batters, drew immediate criticism. By that point Ireland had built the momentum that carried them past 180.

Iyer's captaincy is under early scrutiny. Suryakumar Yadav was not just stripped of the captaincy but dropped from the squad entirely after a lean IPL. Young Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the 18-year-old who scored 776 runs for Rajasthan Royals in IPL 2026, made his first senior trip but did not feature in the playing eleven.

## The Bigger Picture

Ireland's victory is the biggest result in their bilateral cricket history since they beat the West Indies 2-1 in an ODI series in 2022. Only four players from that squad featured in Friday's eleven.

For India, the defeat is a sharp reminder that the transition between eras is rarely smooth. The team that won the T20 World Cup in March has already lost several senior players to retirement or rest. What remains is a squad still learning its combinations, now facing a must-win second T20I at the same Belfast ground today, Sunday, before heading to England for an eight-match tour starting July 1.

Gambhir has called for optional nets on the rest day — a move that suggests the coaching staff is treating Friday's result as more than a one-off aberration.

For the Indian diaspora across the UK and Ireland — tens of thousands of whom follow India's away tours with the fervour of a second home crowd — the loss stings. But for the Irish cricket community, many of whom have Indian-origin members, it is a moment of genuine sporting history. Belfast's Civil Service Cricket Club, a venue more accustomed to hosting club matches, can now claim the site of India's first-ever defeat to Ireland in international cricket.
